implementation_notes: Optional is the Maybe instance: of/ofNullable is unit, map transforms a present value, and flatMap takes a function that returns another Optional (bind), keeping the first empty Optional as the short-circuit; Stream.flatMap is the same operation for the List/multi-valued instance, with laziness playing the role of deferred effects. Java has no Monad interface and no higher-kinded types, so each effect type (Optional, Stream, CompletableFuture) spells bind under its own name; a general monad class is justified only when a library such as Vavr is already in the stack.
code_sketch:
Optional<City> city =
    Optional.ofNullable(userId)
        .flatMap(users::find)        // bind: empty stays empty
        .map(User::address)
        .flatMap(Address::city);     // depends on the previous value
pitfalls: Optional is a return-type idiom, not a general container: the JDK docs discourage fields and parameters of that type, and get() reintroduces the failure it was meant to remove.
Stream.flatMap is lazy, so a 'step' with side effects runs only when a terminal operation executes - often far from the chain that built it.
Mixing effect types (Optional inside CompletableFuture) needs explicit bridging with thenApply/flatMap, which is where transformer-style nesting begins.

variants.name: CompletableFuture.thenCompose chains
variants.implementation_notes: thenApply is map and thenCompose is flatMap: it takes a function returning another CompletionStage, flattens it and adopts its completion, so a request whose next call depends on the previous response is one chain instead of a callback pyramid. Failures travel inside the stage, so they are handled with exceptionally/handle rather than try/catch. Prefer it for stage-based composition a framework already returns; for blocking-style dependent I/O on Java 21, virtual threads read better.
variants.code_sketch:
CompletableFuture<Report> report =
    users.findAsync(userId)                       // CompletableFuture<User>
        .thenCompose(user -> orders.of(user))     // bind, not thenApply
        .thenApply(this::summarize);              // map: plain value
pitfalls: thenApply with a function that returns a CompletionStage yields CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<T>>; the compiler accepts it and the chain silently nests.
Stages run on ForkJoinPool.commonPool() by default: blocking calls inside them starve the pool and degrade unrelated parallel work.
thenComposeAsync vs thenCompose changes which thread runs the function; mixing them without an explicit executor makes thread use unpredictable.

variants.name: Virtual threads + structured concurrency (IO as blocking calls)
variants.implementation_notes: Java 21's virtual threads make an explicit IO monad unnecessary: threads become cheap enough for a task per operation, so dependent I/O is written as ordinary blocking calls inside a virtual thread and failure propagation stays with exceptions. Prefer this for server code whose only effect is I/O; keep Optional/CompletableFuture chaining for in-memory absence and for composing stages a framework already returns.
pitfalls: Pinning: synchronized blocks (and native frames) can pin a virtual thread to its carrier and destroy scalability; prefer ReentrantLock.
Virtual threads increase throughput, not speed: CPU-bound work does not get faster and should stay on a bounded pool.
Thread-local caches and pooled resources sized for platform threads become unbounded when one virtual thread per task is the default.
